section.heading: 5.5 Complex Eigenvalues
section.paragraph: Since the characteristic equation of an $$n \times n$$ matrix involves a polynomial of degree $$n$$ , the equation always has exactly $$n$$ roots, counting multiplicities, provided that possibly complex roots are included. This section shows that if the characteristic equation of a real matrix $$A$$ has some complex roots, then these roots provide critical information about $$A$$ . The key is to let $$A$$ act on the space $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ of $$n \text{-tuples}$$ of complex numbers.1

Our interest in $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ does not arise from a desire to “generalize” the results of the earlier chapters, although that would in fact open up significant new applications of linear algebra.2 Rather, this study of complex eigenvalues is essential in order to uncover “hidden” information about certain matrices with real entries that arise in a variety of real-life problems. Such problems include many real dynamical systems that involve periodic motion, vibration, or some type of rotation in space.

The matrix eigenvalue–eigenvector theory already developed for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ applies equally well to $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ . So a complex scalar $$\text{λ}$$ satisfies $$\det (A - \text{λ} I) = 0$$ if and only if there is a nonzero vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ such that $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ . We call $$\text{λ}$$ a (complex) eigenvalue and $$\textbf{x}$$ a (complex) eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 0 & {- 1} \\ 1 & 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then the linear transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ on $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ rotates the plane counterclockwise through a quarter-turn. The action of $$A$$ is periodic, since after four quarter-turns, a vector is back where it started. Obviously, no nonzero vector is mapped into a multiple of itself, so $$A$$ has no eigenvectors in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ and hence no real eigenvalues. In fact, the characteristic equation of $$A$$ is
The only roots are complex: $$\text{λ} = i$$ and $$\text{λ} = - i$$ . However, if we permit $$A$$ to act on $$\textbf{\mathbb{C}}^{2}$$ , then

$$& \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ - i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}i \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = i \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ - i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- i \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = - i \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ i\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

Thus $$i$$ and $$- i$$ are eigenvalues, with $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- i} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ i \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ as corresponding eigenvectors. (A method for finding complex eigenvectors is discussed in Example 2.)

section.paragraph: The main focus of this section will be on the matrix in the next example.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} .5 & {{- .}6} \\ .75 & 1.1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find the eigenvalues of $$A$$ , and find a basis for each eigenspace.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The characteristic equation of $$A$$ is

$$0 = det \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 - \lambda & - .6 \\ .75 & 1.1 - \lambda\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \left(\right. .5 - \lambda \left.\right) \left(\right. 1.1 - \lambda \left.\right) - \left(\right. - .6 \left.\right) \left(\right. .75 \left.\right) & = \lambda^{2} - 1.6 \lambda + 1$$
From the quadratic formula, $$\text{λ} = \frac{1}{2}\lbrack 1.6 \pm \sqrt{( - 1.6)^{2} - 4}\rbrack = .8 \pm .6i$$ . For the eigenvalue $$\text{λ} = .8 - .6i$$ , construct

$$A - \left(\right. .8 - .6 i \left.\right) I & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.5 & - .6 \\ .75 & 1.1\end{matrix} \left]\right. - \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.8 - .6 i & 0 \\ 0 & .8 - .6 i\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- .3 + .6 i & - .6 \\ .75 & .3 + .6 i\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

Row reduction of the usual augmented matrix is quite unpleasant by hand because of the complex arithmetic. However, here is a nice observation that really simplifies matters: Since $$.8 - .6i$$ is an eigenvalue, the system
$$\left(\right. - .3 + .6 i \left.\right) x_{1} - & .6 x_{2} & = 0 .75 x_{1} + & \left(\right. .3 + 6 i \left.\right) x_{2} & = 0$$

has a nontrivial solution (with $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ possibly complex numbers). Therefore, both equations in (2) determine the same relationship between $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ , and either equation can be used to express one variable in terms of the other.3
The second equation in (2) leads to
$$.75 x_{1} & = \left(\right. - .3 - .6 i \left.\right) x_{2} x_{1} & = \left(\right. - .4 - .8 i \left.\right) x_{2}$$
Choose $$x_{2} = 5$$ to eliminate the decimals, and obtain $$x_{1} = - 2 - 4i$$ . A basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $$\text{λ} = .8 - .6i$$ is
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 - 4 i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
Analogous calculations for $$\text{λ} = .8 + .6i$$ produce the eigenvector
$$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 + 4 i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
As a check on the work, compute

$$A \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} .5 & - .6 \\ .75 & 1.1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} - 2 + 4 i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 4 + 2 i \\ 4 + 3 i \end{bmatrix} = \left(\right. .8 + .6 i \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{2}$$

section.paragraph: Surprisingly, the matrix $$A$$ in Example 2 determines a transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ that is essentially a rotation. This fact becomes evident when appropriate points are plotted, as illustrated in Figure 1.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: One way to see how multiplication by the matrix $$A$$ in Example 2 affects points is to plot an arbitrary initial point—say, $$\textbf{x}_{0} = (2,0)$$ —and then to plot successive images of this point under repeated multiplications by $$A$$ . That is, plot

$$\textbf{x}_{1} & = A \textbf{x}_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 & - .6 \\ .75 & 1.1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 \\ 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1.0 \\ 1.5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{2} & = A \textbf{x}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 & - .6 \\ .75 & 1.1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1.0 \\ 1.5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- .4 \\ 2.4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{3} & = A \textbf{x}_{2} , \ldots$$

Figure 1 shows $$\textbf{x}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{8}$$ as larger dots. The smaller dots are the locations of $$\textbf{x}_{9} , \ldots ,$$ $$\textbf{x}_{100}$$ . The sequence lies along an elliptical orbit.
example.heading: Figure 1
example.paragraph: Iterates of a point $$\mathbf{x}_{0}$$ under the action of a matrix with a complex eigenvalue

section.paragraph: Of course, Figure 1 does not explain why the rotation occurs. The secret to the rotation is hidden in the real and imaginary parts of a complex eigenvector.
section.heading: Real and Imaginary Parts of Vectors
section.paragraph: The complex conjugate of a complex vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ is the vector $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ in $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ whose entries are the complex conjugates of the entries in $$\textbf{x}$$ . The real part and imaginary parts of a complex vector $$\textbf{x}$$ are the vectors $$\textbf{Re}\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{Im}\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ formed from the real and imaginary parts of the entries of $$\textbf{x}$$ . Thus,
$$\boxed{\textbf{x} = \text{Re} \textbf{x} + \textit{i} \text{Im} \textbf{x}}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If $$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} {3 - i} \\ i \\ {2 + 5i} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + i\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then

$$\text{Re} \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \text{Im} \textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} \bar{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} - i \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 + i \\ - i \\ 2 - 5 i \end{bmatrix}$$

section.paragraph: If $$B$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix with possibly complex entries, then $$\overset{‾}{B}$$ denotes the matrix whose entries are the complex conjugates of the entries in $$B$$ . Let $$r$$ be a complex number and $$\textbf{x}$$ any vector. Properties of conjugates for complex numbers carry over to complex matrix algebra:
$$\bar{r \mathbf{x}} = \bar{r} \bar{\textbf{x}} , & \bar{B \textbf{x}} = \bar{B} \bar{\textbf{x}} , & \bar{B C} = \bar{B} \bar{C} , & \text{and} & \bar{r B} = \bar{r} \bar{B}$$
section.heading: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Real Matrix That Acts on ℂn
section.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$n \times n$$ matrix whose entries are real. Then $$\overset{‾}{A\textbf{x}} = \overset{‾}{A}\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}} = A\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ . If $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ and $$\textbf{x}$$ is a corresponding eigenvector in $$\mathbb{C}^{n}$$ , then
$$A \bar{x} = \bar{A x} = \bar{\lambda x} = \bar{\lambda} \bar{x}$$

Hence $$\overset{‾}{ \text{λ} }$$ is also an eigenvalue of $$A$$ , with $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$$ a corresponding eigenvector. This shows that when $$A$$ is real, its complex eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. (Here and elsewhere, we use the term complex eigenvalue to refer to an eigenvalue $$\text{λ} = a + bi$$ , with $$b \neq 0$$ .)

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: The eigenvalues of the real matrix in Example 2 are complex conjugates, namely $$.8 - .6i$$ and $$.8 + .6i$$ . The corresponding eigenvectors found in Example 2 are also conjugates:
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 - 4 i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 + 4 i \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \left(\overset{\overline}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{1}$$

section.paragraph: The next example provides the basic “building block” for all real $$2 \times 2$$ matrices with complex eigenvalues.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: If $$C = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & {- b} \\ b & a \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , where $$a$$ and $$b$$ are real and not both zero, then the eigenvalues of $$C$$ are $$\text{λ} = a \pm bi$$ . (See the Practice Problem at the end of this section.) Also, if $$r = | \text{λ} | = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}$$ , then

$$C = r \begin{bmatrix} a / r & - b / r \\ b / r & a / r \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} cos \varphi & - sin \varphi \\ sin \varphi & cos \varphi \end{bmatrix}$$

where $$\varphi$$ is the angle between the positive $$x \text{-axis}$$ and the ray from $$(0,0)$$ through $$(a,b)$$ . See Figure 2 and Appendix B. The angle $$\varphi$$ is called the argument of $$\text{λ} = a + bi$$ . Thus the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto C\textbf{x}$$ may be viewed as the composition of a rotation through the angle $$\varphi$$ and a scaling by $$| \text{λ} |$$ (see Figure 3).

image.alt: A graph shows a right-angled triangle in the first quadrant. The adjacent side is on the horizontal axis. The left end of the adjacent side is on the origin.
A graph shows scaling up as well as rotating a vector x. The graph consists of two vectors starting from the origin pointing in the second quadrant with one being smaller than the other.

figure.caption: Figure 3 A rotation followed by a scaling

section.paragraph: Finally, we are ready to uncover the rotation that is hidden within a real matrix having a complex eigenvalue.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} .5 & {{- .}6} \\ .75 & 1.1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\text{λ} = .8 - .6i$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2 - 4i} \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , as in Example 2. Also, let $$P$$ be the $$2 \times 2$$ real matrix, described in Theorem 9,
$$P = \begin{bmatrix} \text{Re} \textbf{v}_{1} & \text{Im} \textbf{v}_{1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 & - 4 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
and let

$$C = P^{- 1} A P = \frac{1}{20} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ - 5 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} .5 & - . 6 \\ .75 & 1.1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} - 2 & - 4 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .8 & - . 6 \\ .6 & .8 \end{bmatrix}$$
By Example 6, $$C$$ is a pure rotation because $$| \text{λ} |^{2} = (.8)^{2} + (.6)^{2} = 1$$ . From $$C = P^{- 1}AP$$ , we obtain
$$A = P C P^{- 1} = P \begin{bmatrix} .8 & - . 6 \\ .6 & .8 \end{bmatrix} P^{- 1}$$

Here is the rotation “inside” $$A$$ ! The matrix $$P$$ provides a change of variable, say, $$\textbf{x} = P\textbf{u}$$ . The action of $$A$$ amounts to a change of variable from $$\textbf{x}$$ to $$\textbf{u}$$ , followed by a rotation, and then a return to the original variable. See Figure 4. The rotation produces an ellipse, as in Figure 1, instead of a circle, because the coordinate system determined by the columns of $$P$$ is not rectangular and does not have equal unit lengths on the two axes.

image.alt: A figure shows four arrows forming a rectangle having different matrix notations on its vertices.

figure.caption: Figure 4 Rotation due to a complex eigenvalue

section.paragraph: The next theorem shows that the calculations in Example 7 can be carried out for any $$2 \times 2$$ real matrix $$A$$ having a complex eigenvalue $$\text{λ}$$ . The proof uses the fact that if the entries in $$A$$ are real, then $$A\left( \text{Re} \textbf{x} \right) = \text{Re} \left( A\textbf{x} \right)$$ and $$A\left( \text{Im} \textbf{x} \right) = \text{Im} \left( A\textbf{x} \right)$$ , and if $$\textbf{x}$$ is an eigenvector for a complex eigenvalue, then $$\text{Re} \textbf{x}$$ and $$\text{Im} \textbf{x}$$ are linearly independent in $$\textbf{R}^{2}$$ . (See Exercises 29 and 30.) The details are omitted.

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
note.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be a real $$2 \times 2$$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue $$\text{λ} = a - bi(b \neq 0)$$ and an associated eigenvector v in $$\mathbb{C}^{2}$$ . Then

$$A = P C P^{- 1} , \text{where} P = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix} \text{Re} \textbf{v} & \text{Im} \textbf{v}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \text{and} C = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a & - b \\ b & a\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

section.paragraph: The phenomenon displayed in Example 7 persists in higher dimensions. For instance, if $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue, then there is a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ on which $$A$$ acts as a rotation (possibly combined with scaling). Every vector in that plane is rotated into another point on the same plane. We say that the plane is invariant under $$A$$ .

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: The matrix $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrc} .8 & {{- .}6} & 0 \\ .6 & {.8} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {1.07} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ has eigenvalues $$.8 \pm .6i$$ and $$1.07$$ . Any vector $$\textbf{w}_{0}$$ in the $$x_{1}x_{2} \text{-plane}$$ (with third coordinate $$0$$ ) is rotated by $$A$$ into another point in the plane. Any vector $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ not in the plane has its $$x_{3} \text{-coordinate}$$ multiplied by $$1.07$$ . The iterates of the points $$\textbf{w}_{0} = (2,0,0)$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{0} = (2,0,1)$$ under multiplication by $$A$$ are shown in Figure 5.

image.alt: A graph shows a hollow cylinder placed around the z axis with a spiral curve along its surface. The centerline of the hollow cylinder coincides with the z axis.

figure.caption: Figure 5 Iterates of two points under the action of a 3×3 matrix with a complex eigenvalue

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Many robots work by rotating at various joints, just as matrices with complex eigenvalues rotate points in space. Figure 6 illustrates a robot arm made using linear transformations, each with a pair of complex eigenvalues. In Project C, at the end of the chapter, you will be asked to find videos of robots on the web that use rotations as a key element of their functioning.

section.paragraph: 1 Refer to Appendix B for a brief discussion of complex numbers. Matrix algebra and concepts about real vector spaces carry over to the case with complex entries and scalars. In particular, $$A(c\textbf{x} + d\textbf{y}) = cA\textbf{x} + dA\textbf{y}$$ , for $$A$$ an $$m \times n$$ matrix with complex entries, $$\textbf{x}$$ , $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{C}}^{n}$$ , and $$c$$ , $$d$$ in $$\mathbf{C}$$ .
2 A second course in linear algebra often discusses such topics. They are of particular importance in electrical engineering.
